beats.text: Before fingerprints. Before DNA. Before anyone had a word for forensic science at all --
there was just a hunch, and a body, and no way to prove either one.
This is CipherStudios. These are the first five times science ever caught a killer.
Five techniques. Five people who never met each other. A hundred and forty-eight years apart.
Every single one of them -- the first time it had ever been done.
Welcome to Case File 002.
Le Glandier, France. 1840. Charles Lafarge is dying -- slowly -- and his young wife Marie is the one bringing him his food.
Doctors suspect arsenic. The problem: in 1840, there's no reliable way to prove poison in a body, only in a cup.
So chemist Mathieu Orfila does something no courtroom has seen before -- the Marsh test, turning invisible poison into a visible mirror of metal on glass.
The result: undeniable arsenic. Marie Lafarge is convicted on forensic chemistry alone -- the first time in history.
France is still arguing about whether Orfila got it right.
Necochea, Argentina. A mother, cut at the throat. Her two children, dead beside her.
She blamed a neighbor. The police believed her -- for one day.
Then someone noticed the bloody thumbprint on the bedroom door -- it didn't belong to the neighbor at all.
It matched the file Inspector Alvarez had just built.
A system no one had ever used to solve a murder before.
Confronted with her own thumb, Francisca Rojas confessed.
West Shelby, New York. 1915. Charles Stielow is found with his boss's housekeeper dead beside him.
A firearms expert told the jury Stielow's revolver fired the fatal bullets. He was five weeks from the electric chair.
There was one problem -- the expert had never actually compared the bullets to the gun.
A real forensic ballistics exam, under a comparison microscope, found the bullets didn't match his gun at all.
The wrong man walked free. Ballistics testimony would never be taken on faith again.
New York City. 1956. For sixteen years, a bomber has planted devices across the city and vanished every time.
Police call in psychiatrist James Brussel. He predicts a foreign-born man, in his forties, a grudge against Con Edison.
He even predicts the suit -- buttoned, double-breasted -- the bomber will be wearing when they find him.
They arrest George Metesky. He's wearing exactly that suit.
Leicestershire, England. 1988. Two girls murdered three years apart. Police test every man in three villages.
The same new test -- DNA fingerprinting -- had already cleared an innocent teenager months earlier.
Colin Pitchfork paid a friend to give blood in his place. The swap itself was the tell.
When it unraveled, his own sample matched both girls.
Five techniques. Five countries. A hundred and forty-eight years.
Every one of them started the same way -- as somebody's untested hunch.
This has been Case File 002. If you want to be here for Case File 003, subscribe. CipherStudios.
